questions.question: Which of these errors WILL an error boundary catch?
options: An error thrown inside an onClick event handler
An error thrown inside a setTimeout callback
An error thrown during a child component's render
A rejected Promise from a fetch call
questions.explanation: Error boundaries only catch errors thrown during rendering, lifecycle methods, and constructors in the tree below them — not in event handlers or async callbacks.

questions.question: Why must an error boundary still be written as a class component?
options: The required lifecycle methods, getDerivedStateFromError and componentDidCatch, have no hook equivalent
It's just a historical convention with no technical reason
questions.explanation: There is no hook version of getDerivedStateFromError/componentDidCatch, so error boundaries remain one of the few cases where a class component is required.

questions.question: What does `<Suspense fallback={<Spinner />}>` do?
options: Shows the fallback while a wrapped component (e.g. lazy-loaded) is still loading, then swaps in the real content
Retries a failed network request automatically
Delays rendering for a fixed timeout
questions.explanation: Suspense lets a component 'pause' rendering until its dependency (like a lazy-loaded chunk) is ready, showing the fallback in the meantime.

questions.question: What does `React.lazy(() => import("./ProductDetails"))` achieve?
options: It disables the component entirely in production
It code-splits ProductDetails into a separate bundle loaded only when it's rendered
It converts ProductDetails into a Server Component
questions.explanation: React.lazy defers loading a component's code until it's actually needed, reducing the initial bundle size — paired with Suspense to show a loading state meanwhile.
